claim: The vomeronasal organ (VNO) serves as a primary sensory channel for detecting predator cues by relaying signals to the medial hypothalamic nuclei, particularly the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), which directly controls defensive behavioral outputs.
source: The vomeronasal organ (VNO) serves as a primary sensory channel for detecting predator cues by relaying signals to the medial hypothalamic nuclei, particularly the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), which directly controls defensive behavioral outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the VNO-VMH pathway and its role in defensive behavior.

claim: Cat saliva contains predator cues that signal the imminence of predator threat and modulate the intensity of freezing behavior through the VNO in mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that cat saliva contains predator cues that signal the imminence of predator threat and modulate the intensity of freezing behavior through the VNO in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral experiments and neural activation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cat saliva activates VNO neurons expressing the V2R-A4 subfamily of sensory receptors.
source: Cat saliva activates VNO neurons expressing the V2R-A4 subfamily of sensory receptors, and the number of VNO neurons activated in response to saliva correlates with both the freshness of saliva and the intensity of freezing behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing co-localization of V2R-A4 probes with pS6-IR signals in VNO neurons exposed to cat saliva.

claim: The number of VNO neurons activated in response to saliva correlates with both the freshness of saliva and the intensity of freezing behavior.
source: Cat saliva activates VNO neurons expressing the V2R-A4 subfamily of sensory receptors, and the number of VNO neurons activated in response to saliva correlates with both the freshness of saliva and the intensity of freezing behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing a positive correlation (R2 = 0.3586, p=0.0020) between pS6-positive neurons and freezing duration.

claim: The number of VMH neurons activated by fresh, but not old, saliva positively correlates with the intensity of freezing behavior.
source: Moreover, the number of VMH neurons activated by fresh, but not old, saliva positively correlates with the intensity of freezing behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing a significant positive correlation (R2 = 0.5708, p=0.0412) for fresh saliva but not old saliva.

claim: Fresh and old saliva predominantly activate distinct neuronal populations within the VMH.
source: Detailed analyses of the spatial distribution of activated neurons, as well as their overlap within the same individual mice, revealed that fresh and old saliva predominantly activate distinct neuronal populations within the VMH.
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiments showing that only 16% of old saliva-activated cells were reactivated by fresh saliva, compared to 43% for fresh-fresh exposures.

claim: There is an accessory olfactory circuit in mice that is specifically tuned to time-sensitive components of cat saliva, which optimizes their defensive behavior to maximize their chance of survival according to the imminence of threat.
source: Collectively, this study suggests that there is an accessory olfactory circuit in mice that is specifically tuned to time-sensitive components of cat saliva, which optimizes their defensive behavior to maximize their chance of survival according to the imminence of threat.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: Immediacy of the threat, determined by perceived distance from predators, is one of the key factors influencing defensive behavioral decisions, which regulates the intensity of behavioral outputs.
source: Immediacy of the threat, determined by perceived distance from predators, is one of the key factors influencing defensive behavioral decisions, which regulates the intensity of behavioral outputs (Figure 1A; Blanchard and Blanchard, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blanchard and Blanchard, 1989.

claim: In nocturnal animals including rodents, olfaction is one of the major sensory modalities by which predator-derived chemical cues are detected.
source: In nocturnal animals including rodents, olfaction is one of the major sensory modalities by which predator-derived chemical cues are detected (Apfelbach et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Apfelbach et al., 2005.

claim: Rodents respond to a variety of predator-derived chemical cues, such as odors from fox feces, snake skin, cat fur, and cat collars, in both the field and laboratory environments.
source: Rodents respond to a variety of predator-derived chemical cues, such as odors from fox feces, snake skin, cat fur, and cat collars, in both the field and laboratory environments (Apfelbach et al., 2005; Kats and Dill, 1998; Papes et al., 2010; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2015; Takahashi, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice exposed to fresh saliva exhibited considerably longer freezing episodes, accounting for over 50% of the total duration of observation, whereas those exposed to old saliva exhibited freezing episodes for less than 20% of the total duration on average.
source: Mice exposed to fresh saliva exhibited considerably longer freezing episodes, accounting for over 50% of the total duration of observation, whereas those exposed to old saliva exhibited freezing episodes for less than 20% of the total duration on average (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (One-way ANOVA, p<0.0001).

claim: The latency to the first contact was slightly longer for fresh saliva compared to old saliva.
source: The latency to the first contact was slightly longer for saliva collected immediately before introduction to the mouse cage (fresh saliva) compared to that for saliva collected a few hours prior to the behavior test (old saliva) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance (p=0.0089).

claim: Mice exposed to a swab containing either fresh or old saliva significantly avoided interacting with the swab, while mice exposed to a clean control swab spent a significant amount of time directly interacting with the swab to investigate it.
source: On the contrary, mice exposed to a swab containing either fresh or old saliva significantly avoided interacting with the swab, while mice exposed to a clean control swab spent a significant amount of time directly interacting with the swab to investigate it, including direct sniffing and chewing (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis (One-way ANOVA, p<0.0001).

claim: The stress hormone adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) in plasma showed a trend toward twofold upregulation after exposure to both fresh and old saliva.
source: Additionally, the stress hormone adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) in plasma showed a trend toward twofold upregulation after exposure to both fresh and old saliva (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis (One-way ANOVA, p=0.0381).

claim: The saliva volumes at the time of behavioral testing were indistinguishable between fresh and old samples.
source: Saliva-containing swabs were kept in sealed containers immediately after collection from cats to prevent evaporation, ensuring that the saliva volumes at the time of behavioral testing were indistinguishable between fresh and old samples (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by volume measurement data shown in Figure 1I (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.1949).

claim: The concentrations of total proteins in both fresh and old saliva were indiscernible, which was approximately 1.5 μg/μL.
source: The concentrations of total proteins in both fresh and old saliva were also indiscernible, which was approximately 1.5 μg/μL (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein concentration measurement data shown in Figure 1J (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.7518).

claim: The amount of Fel d 4, one of the most abundant proteins in saliva, was nearly equivalent between fresh and old saliva.
source: Furthermore, the amount of Fel d 4, one of the most abundant proteins in saliva, was nearly equivalent between fresh and old saliva (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the differences between fresh and old cat saliva lie in specific components rather than the total or major saliva content.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to diluted fresh saliva resulted in a shorter duration of freezing behavior.
source: Indeed, exposure to diluted fresh saliva resulted in a shorter duration of freezing behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1K comparing different dilutions of fresh saliva.

claim: Fresh saliva diluted to 70% induced freezing behavior for a duration equivalent to that of undiluted fresh saliva, while freezing behavior in response to 50 and 30% fresh saliva was significantly reduced to the same duration as that observed with old saliva.
source: Fresh saliva diluted to 70% induced freezing behavior for a duration equivalent to that of undiluted fresh saliva, while freezing behavior in response to 50 and 30% fresh saliva was significantly reduced to the same duration as that observed with old saliva (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1K with statistical analysis.

claim: Cat saliva contains predator cues that attenuate over time, which is detected by mice to assess the imminence of predator threat and modulate defensive behavioral outputs.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that cat saliva contains predator cues that attenuate over time, which is detected by mice to assess the imminence of predator threat and modulate defensive behavioral outputs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral and biochemical data presented.

claim: Fresh saliva is recognized as an immediate danger and induces more robust freezing behavior, while old saliva is recognized as a less immediate danger and induces less robust freezing behavioral responses.
source: More specifically, fresh saliva is recognized as an immediate danger and induces more robust freezing behavior, while old saliva is recognized as a less immediate danger and induces less robust freezing behavioral responses.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the differential behavioral responses to fresh versus old saliva.

claim: When a container containing a swab with fresh saliva was introduced into the home cage, the mice no longer exhibited freezing behavior toward the container, but instead directly investigated it similarly to the control swab-containing container.
source: Interestingly, we found that when we introduced a container containing a swab with fresh saliva into the home cage, the mice no longer exhibited freezing behavior toward the container, but instead directly investigated it similarly to the control swab-containing container (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A and B (Two-tailed t-test, p=0.9311 for freezing).

claim: Freezing behavior requires direct contact with the saliva-containing swab and the freezing-inducing cues in cat saliva detected in this scheme are nonvolatile.
source: This suggests that freezing behavior requires direct contact with the saliva-containing swab and that the freezing-inducing cues in cat saliva detected in this scheme are nonvolatile.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experiment showing no freezing when direct contact is prevented.

claim: Trpc2-KO mice failed to exhibit freezing behavior upon exposure to a fresh saliva-containing swab, in contrast to their wild-type littermates who displayed freezing responses.
source: Upon exposure to a fresh saliva-containing swab, Trpc2-KO mice failed to exhibit freezing behavior, in contrast to their wild-type littermates who displayed freezing responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C comparing Trpc2-WT and Trpc2-KO mice (Two-way ANOVA with Tukey's test, p=0.0037).

claim: Trpc2-KO mice directly investigated the saliva swab with a similar level of intensity as the control swab, while the wild-type littermates actively avoided it.
source: Additionally, the Trpc2-KO mice directly investigated the saliva swab with a similar level of intensity as the control swab, while the wild-type littermates actively avoided it (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D (Two-way ANOVA with Tukey's test, p=0.0003).

claim: VNO activation, disrupted in Trpc2-KO mice, is necessary for the freezing behavior observed in response to cat saliva in mice.
source: These findings suggest that VNO activation, disrupted in Trpc2-KO mice, is necessary for the freezing behavior observed in response to cat saliva in mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Trpc2-KO behavioral data.

claim: Exposure to both fresh and old cat saliva induced an increase in pS6-IR in the basal VNO neurons that express Gαo protein.
source: We observed that exposure to both fresh and old cat saliva induced an increase in pS6-IR in the basal VNO neurons that express Gαo protein (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: pS6-IR was rarely observed in the apical VNO neurons.
source: Conversely, pS6-IR was rarely observed in the apical VNO neurons (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F (One-way ANOVA, p=0.1010).

claim: The number of pS6-positive neurons was more than three times higher in mice exposed to fresh saliva compared to that exposed to old saliva.
source: Notably, we found that the number of pS6-positive neurons was more than three times higher in mice exposed to fresh saliva compared to that exposed to old saliva (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G (One-way ANOVA, p<0.0001).

claim: There is a significantly positive correlation (R2 = 0.3586, 95% CI [0.2458, 0.8116], p=0.0020) between the numbers of active sensory neurons and behavioral outputs.
source: Strikingly, when the duration of freezing was plotted as a function of pS6-IR signals in the VNO of individual animals, we observed a significantly positive correlation (R2 = 0.3586, 95% CI [0.2458, 0.8116], p=0.0020) between the numbers of active sensory neurons and behavioral outputs (Figure 2H), suggesting that more intense freezing behavior is induced when more VNO neurons are activated by cat saliva.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Freezing-inducing predator cues are detected by Gαo-positive sensory neurons in the VNO, and these sensory neurons convey the imminence of predator threat to higher brain centers.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that freezing-inducing predator cues are detected by Gαo-positive sensory neurons in the VNO, and these sensory neurons convey the imminence of predator threat to higher brain centers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the VNO activation data.

claim: The basal VNO neurons express sensory receptors that belong to vomeronasal receptor type 2 (V2R) family of G protein-coupled receptors in mice.
source: The basal VNO neurons express sensory receptors that belong to vomeronasal receptor type 2 (V2R) family of G protein-coupled receptors in mice (Figure 3A; Mohrhardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mohrhardt et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The mouse V2R family consists of over 120 intact genes, which are divided into V2R A1-6, A8-10, and B-D subfamilies based on sequence homology.
source: The mouse V2R family consists of over 120 intact genes, which are divided into V2R A1-6, A8-10, and B-D subfamilies based on sequence homology (Figure 3A; Francia et al., 2014; Silvotti et al., 2011; Silvotti et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Francia et al., 2014; Silvotti et al., 2011; Silvotti et al., 2007.

claim: With the exception of the V2R C group that is co-expressed with other groups of V2Rs in the basal VNO neurons, each sensory neuron expresses only one member of the V2R receptor, allowing individual neurons to respond to specific molecules.
source: With the exception of the V2R C group that is co-expressed with other groups of V2Rs in the basal VNO neurons, each sensory neuron expresses only one member of the V2R receptor, allowing individual neurons to respond to specific molecules (Mohrhardt et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mohrhardt et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately 45% of pS6-IR signals induced by fresh saliva (83 out of 181) co-localized with V2R-A4 probe signals.
source: Approximately 45% of pS6-IR signals induced by fresh saliva (83 out of 181) co-localized with V2R-A4 probe signals, with less than 1% of pS6-IR (1 out of 120) co-localized with A8-4 probe signals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: V2R-A4 probe signals also co-localized with approximately 45% of pS6-IR signals induced by old saliva (37 out of 86).
source: Notably, V2R-A4 probe signals also co-localized with approximately 45% of pS6-IR signals induced by old saliva (37 out of 86).
evidence: This claim is supported by dual staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: None of the other probe signals co-localized with pS6-IR induced by both fresh and old saliva.
source: None of the other probe signals co-localized with pS6-IR induced by both fresh and old saliva.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Members of the V2R-A4 subfamily are potential sensory receptors for the predator cues contained in both fresh and old cat saliva.
source: These results indicate that members of the V2R-A4 subfamily are potential sensory receptors for the predator cues contained in both fresh and old cat saliva, and varying levels of imminence of predator threat stimulate the same type of sensory receptors in a quantitatively different manner to regulate the freezing behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-localization data.

claim: Varying levels of imminence of predator threat stimulate the same type of sensory receptors in a quantitatively different manner to regulate the freezing behavior.
source: These results indicate that members of the V2R-A4 subfamily are potential sensory receptors for the predator cues contained in both fresh and old cat saliva, and varying levels of imminence of predator threat stimulate the same type of sensory receptors in a quantitatively different manner to regulate the freezing behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that both fresh and old saliva activate V2R-A4 neurons but in different quantities.

claim: The activation of the basal VNO neurons by cat saliva leads to predominant induction of cFos-IR signals in the pAOB, whose glomerulus layer is Gαi-IR negative.
source: We found that the activation of the basal VNO neurons by cat saliva leads to predominant induction of cFos-IR signals in the pAOB, whose glomerulus layer is Gαi-IR negative (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: The numbers of cFos-positive mitral and granule cells in the pAOB in saliva-exposed mice are significantly higher than those in mice exposed to the control swab.
source: The numbers of cFos-positive mitral and granule cells in the pAOB in saliva-exposed mice are significantly higher than those in mice exposed to the control swab (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and F with statistical analysis.

claim: There were no differences in the numbers of cFos-positive mitral and granule cells in the AOB between fresh and old saliva-exposed mice.
source: However, contrary to our expectations, we did not observe any differences in the numbers of cFos-positive mitral and granule cells in the AOB between fresh and old saliva-exposed mice (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: Although the AOB processes saliva signals from the VNO following predator cue detection, the relationship between the degree of AOB activation and freezing behavior intensity is nonlinear.
source: These results suggest that, although the AOB processes saliva signals from the VNO following predator cue detection, the relationship between the degree of AOB activation and freezing behavior intensity is nonlinear.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of difference in AOB activation between fresh and old saliva despite different behavioral outputs.

claim: Upon exposure to fresh and old saliva, cFos expression in the MeApv, VMH, and dPAG, but not in the BNST, appeared to be upregulated compared to the control stimulus.
source: Upon exposure to fresh and old saliva, cFos expression in the MeApv, VMH, and dPAG, but not in the BNST, appeared to be upregulated compared to the control stimulus (Figure 4G–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G-J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: cFos expression was significantly increased in the VMH of mice exposed to fresh and old saliva compared to the control.
source: Notably, cFos expression was significantly increased in the VMH of mice exposed to fresh and old saliva compared to the control (Figure 4I), consistent with previous observations that the dorsomedial and central subdivisions of VMH (VMHdm/c) contain subpopulations of neurons that control freezing behavior (Engelke et al., 2021; Kunwar et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4I with statistical analysis (One-way ANOVA, p=0.0033) and citations to prior literature.

claim: There was no difference in the number of cFos-positive cells between the two saliva-exposed groups in the neural substrates tested.
source: However, there was no difference in the number of cFos-positive cells between the two saliva-exposed groups in the neural substrates tested (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G-J.

claim: The relationship between neural activity and behavioral output is more complex in the downstream circuit than in the VNO.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the relationship between neural activity and behavioral output is more complex in the downstream circuit than in the VNO.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of VNO and downstream circuit activation patterns.

claim: Fresh and old cat saliva may differentially activate functionally distinct neural populations within these regions, which in turn leads to quantitatively different freezing behavioral responses.
source: This suggests that fresh and old cat saliva may differentially activate functionally distinct neural populations within these regions, which in turn leads to quantitatively different freezing behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that overall activation levels don't differ but behavioral outputs do.

claim: The numbers of cFos-IR signals in AOB mitral and granule cells, as well as those in neurons in the BNST and dPAG, did not correlate with the duration of freezing behavior in any of the exposure groups.
source: To our surprise, we found that the numbers of cFos-IR signals in AOB mitral and granule cells, as well as those in neurons in the BNST and dPAG, did not correlate with the duration of freezing behavior in any of the exposure groups (Figure 5A–C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A-C and F.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the number of cFos-IR signals and behavior intensity only in the fresh saliva-exposed group in the VMH (R2 = 0.5708, 95% CI [–0.1449, 0.9714], p=0.0412) while no such correlation was observed in the old saliva-exposed group.
source: However, we observed a significant positive correlation between the number of cFos-IR signals and behavior intensity only in the fresh saliva-exposed group in the VMH (R2 = 0.5708, 95% CI [–0.1449, 0.9714], p=0.0412) while no such correlation was observed in the old saliva-exposed group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A similar positive correlation trend was observed in the MeApv (R2 = 0.3854, 95% CI [–0.3845, 0.9525], p=0.0942), although it was not statistically significant possibly due to low sample numbers.
source: We observed a similar positive correlation trend in the MeApv (R2 = 0.3854, 95% CI [–0.3845, 0.9525], p=0.0942), although it was not statistically significant possibly due to low sample numbers (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The numbers of cFos-IR signals induced by fresh and old saliva were significantly different in the section 2 bin 5, as well as the section 3 bin 3 and bin 4, which are adjacent to each other.
source: Strikingly, the numbers of cFos-IR signals induced by fresh and old saliva were significantly different in the section 2 bin 5, as well as the section 3 bin 3 and bin 4, which are adjacent to each other (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a distinct population of neurons clustered in a close proximity within the VMH, which is more sensitive to fresh saliva than old saliva.
source: These results suggest that there is a distinct population of neurons clustered in a close proximity within the VMH, which is more sensitive to fresh saliva than old saliva.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial distribution analysis showing specific bins with differential activation.

claim: This population of neurons in the VMHdm may play a role in inducing robust freezing behavior to fresh cat saliva.
source: This population of neurons in the VMHdm may play a role in inducing robust freezing behavior to fresh cat saliva.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the spatial distribution data.

claim: The neurons that induce robust freezing to fresh saliva and less robust freezing to old saliva reside in the same region of the VMH and may use different mechanisms to encode freezing intensity.
source: Moreover, these results also suggest that the neurons that induce robust freezing to fresh saliva and less robust freezing to old saliva reside in the same region of the VMH and may use different mechanisms to encode freezing intensity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the spatial distribution data.

claim: 43% (mean per animal: 61/143) of the cells activated by fresh saliva during the first exposure were also activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure.
source: Quantification of tdTomato and cFos-IR double-positive cells among tdTomato-labeled cells (Figure 7C) revealed that 43% (mean per animal: 61/143) of the cells activated by fresh saliva during the first exposure were also activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure, whereas only 16% (17/106) of cells activated by old saliva during the first exposure were activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure (p=7.5e–6, chi-square test).
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiment data shown in Figure 7 with statistical analysis (chi-square test, p=7.5e-6).

claim: Only 16% (17/106) of cells activated by old saliva during the first exposure were activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure.
source: Quantification of tdTomato and cFos-IR double-positive cells among tdTomato-labeled cells (Figure 7C) revealed that 43% (mean per animal: 61/143) of the cells activated by fresh saliva during the first exposure were also activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure, whereas only 16% (17/106) of cells activated by old saliva during the first exposure were activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure (p=7.5e–6, chi-square test).
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiment data shown in Figure 7 with statistical analysis (chi-square test, p=7.5e-6).

claim: The difference in the fraction of overlapping cells between fresh and old saliva exposures was maintained when comparing the two groups of animals (p=0.0035, permutation test).
source: The difference in the fraction of overlapping cells between fresh and old saliva exposures was maintained when we compared the two groups of animals (Figure 7D, p=0.0035, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiment data shown in Figure 7D with statistical analysis (permutation test, p=0.0035).

claim: 27% (61/226) of cells activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure were previously activated by fresh saliva, whereas 15% (17/112) of cells activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure were previously activated by old saliva (p=0.015, chi-square test).
source: Additionally, quantification of tdTomato and cFos-IR double-positive cells among cFos-IR cells indicated that 27% (61/226) of cells activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure were previously activated by fresh saliva, whereas 15% (17/112) of cells activated by fresh saliva during the second exposure were previously activated by old saliva (p=0.015, chi-square test).
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiment data with statistical analysis (chi-square test, p=0.015).

claim: The difference in the fraction of overlapping cells between fresh and old saliva exposures was also significant in this analysis (p=0.0060, permutation test).
source: The difference in the fraction of overlapping cells between fresh and old saliva exposures was also significant in this analysis (Figure 7E, p=0.0060, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is supported by double exposure experiment data shown in Figure 7E with statistical analysis (permutation test, p=0.0060).

claim: Fresh and old cat saliva activate largely different populations of neurons within the VMH.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that fresh and old cat saliva activate largely different populations of neurons within the VMH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the double exposure experiment data.

claim: The qualitative properties of predator signals, such as freshness, can induce distinct neural processing and ultimately lead to different defensive behavioral outcomes.
source: Overall, our results suggest that the qualitative properties of predator signals, such as freshness, can induce distinct neural processing and ultimately lead to different defensive behavioral outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the findings in the study.

claim: The VNO is involved in detecting and processing chemosensory predator signals that induce fear-related freezing behavior.
source: This study demonstrates that the VNO is involved in detecting and processing chemosensory predator signals that induce fear-related freezing behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Previous studies have shown that the VNO mediates defensive behaviors against predators that are rather related to anxiety state, such as risk assessment, area avoidance, and reduced exploratory and locomotion behaviors.
source: Previous studies have shown that the VNO mediates defensive behaviors against predators that are rather related to anxiety state, such as risk assessment, area avoidance, and reduced exploratory and locomotion behaviors (Isogai et al., 2011; Papes et al., 2010; Pérez-Gómez et al., 2015; Tsunoda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VNO neurons expressing more than half of vomeronasal receptors and a significant fraction of AOB mitral cells have been shown to be activated by predator-derived samples.
source: This is consistent with the fact that VNO neurons expressing more than half of vomeronasal receptors and a significant fraction of AOB mitral cells have been shown to be activated by predator-derived samples (Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ben-Shaul et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2011.

claim: A cat lipocalin allergen, Fel d 4, has been identified as a trigger for risk assessment defensive behavior in mice.
source: A cat lipocalin allergen, Fel d 4, has been identified as a trigger for risk assessment defensive behavior in mice (Papes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Papes et al., 2010.

claim: Recombinant Fel d 4 protein did not induce freezing behavior.
source: Additionally, we found that recombinant Fel d 4 protein did not induce freezing behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: It is unlikely that Fel d 4 alone is the factor responsible for triggering freezing behavior.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that Fel d 4 alone is the factor responsible for triggering freezing behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Fel d 4 protein and Western blot data.

claim: The V2R-A4 subfamily has been shown to be expressed in the VNO neurons that are activated by biological samples derived from various mammalian predators.
source: The V2R-A4 subfamily has been shown to be expressed in the VNO neurons that are activated by biological samples derived from various mammalian predators (Carvalho et al., 2020; Isogai et al., 2011; Rocha et al., 2024; Tsunoda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is likely that specific members of the V2R-A4 subfamily are the receptors for the predator cues in cat saliva that induce freezing behavior.
source: Therefore, it is likely that specific members of the V2R-A4 subfamily are the receptors for the predator cues in cat saliva that induce freezing behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the V2R-A4 co-localization data.

claim: Dual staining of vomeronasal receptors with immediate early gene products has been effectively utilized to identify receptors for several pheromones.
source: Dual staining of vomeronasal receptors with immediate early gene products has been effectively utilized to identify receptors for several pheromones (Carvalho et al., 2020; Haga et al., 2010; Isogai et al., 2018; Isogai et al., 2011; Itakura et al., 2022; Kimoto et al., 2005; Osakada et al., 2022; Osakada et al., 2018; Tsunoda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sensory signals encoding different imminence of predator threat are differentially processed in the VNO-to-VMH pathway.
source: Our correlation analyses between the number of activated neurons and behavior intensity suggest that sensory signals encoding different imminence of predator threat are differentially processed in the VNO-to-VMH pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analyses.

claim: The differential behavioral responses do not appear to result from global neuromodulations of the neural circuit by stress hormones as differential endocrinological responses were not observed.
source: The differential behavioral responses do not appear to result from global neuromodulations of the neural circuit by stress hormones as differential endocrinological responses were not observed (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ACTH data showing no difference between fresh and old saliva.

claim: The axon terminals of hundreds of VNO neurons expressing the same receptor converge into a few specific glomerulus structures.
source: The axon terminals of hundreds of VNO neurons expressing the same receptor converge into a few specific glomerulus structures (Belluscio et al., 1999; Del Punta et al., 2002; Rodriguez et al., 1999), and, in some cases, neurons expressing receptors in the same subfamily send axons into the same glomeruli (Wagner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual AOB mitral cells extend multiple primary dendrites into multiple glomeruli.
source: Individual AOB mitral cells extend multiple primary dendrites into multiple glomeruli (Imamura et al., 2020; Larriva-Sahd, 2008; Takami and Graziadei, 1991; Wagner et al., 2006; Yonekura and Yokoi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Efferent axons of the mitral cells project to multiple brain substrates, namely the BNST, the MEA, and the posteromedial cortical amygdaloid nucleus (PMCo).
source: In turn, efferent axons of the mitral cells project to multiple brain substrates, namely the BNST, the MEA, and the posteromedial cortical amygdaloid nucleus (PMCo) (Davis et al., 1978; Von Campenhausen and Mori, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 1978; Von Campenhausen and Mori, 2000.

claim: Fresh saliva activates more V2R-A4-expressing VNO neurons than old saliva, which may result in stronger activation of V2R-A4 glomeruli in fresh saliva-exposed mice compared to those exposed to old saliva.
source: Fresh saliva activates more V2R-A4-expressing VNO neurons than old saliva, which may result in stronger activation of V2R-A4 glomeruli in fresh saliva-exposed mice compared to those exposed to old saliva.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the VNO activation data.

claim: Differential activations of V2R-A4 glomeruli between fresh and old saliva result in the differential activation of VMH neurons.
source: We assume that such differential activations of V2R-A4 glomeruli between fresh and old saliva result in the differential activation of VMH neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative inference illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The imminent predator cues present in cat saliva activate a specific subpopulation of VMH neurons, whose overall activity positively correlates with the intensity of freezing behavioral outputs.
source: Our findings indicate that the imminent predator cues present in cat saliva activate a specific subpopulation of VMH neurons, whose overall activity positively correlates with the intensity of freezing behavioral outputs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The less imminent predator cues activate a subpopulation of VMH neurons, whose overall activity does not correlate with the intensity of freezing behavior.
source: In contrast, the less imminent predator cues activate a subpopulation of VMH neurons, whose overall activity does not correlate with the intensity of freezing behavior (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Induction of robust freezing behavior is determined by a distinct set of VMH neurons, and the intensity of freezing behavior is encoded separately, possibly by the intensity or dynamics of the neuronal firing.
source: These findings suggest that induction of robust freezing behavior is determined by a distinct set of VMH neurons, and the intensity of freezing behavior is encoded separately, possibly by the intensity or dynamics of the neuronal firing, which cannot be detected by the cFos-IR used in this study.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the correlation data.

claim: The VMHdm/c region contains several subpopulations of neurons that coordinate various defensive behavioral responses.
source: The VMHdm/c region contains several subpopulations of neurons that coordinate various defensive behavioral responses (Engelke et al., 2021; Esteban Masferrer et al., 2020; Kennedy et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2016; Tobias et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of VMHdm/c neurons induces freezing/immobility responses, suggesting that these neurons mediate freezing behavior in response to predator cues.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that optogenetic stimulation of VMHdm/c neurons induces freezing/immobility responses, suggesting that these neurons mediate freezing behavior in response to predator cues (Kunwar et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kunwar et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Imminent predator cues in cat saliva may activate specific neurons with certain excitation levels to directly induce robust freezing behavior, while less imminent predator cues in cat saliva may use a different mechanism to regulate freezing behavior.
source: Therefore, we propose that imminent predator cues in cat saliva may activate these specific neurons with certain excitation levels to directly induce robust freezing behavior, while less imminent predator cues in cat saliva may use a different mechanism to regulate freezing behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the spatial distribution and correlation data.

claim: Selective activation of the VMHdm/c-to-PAG pathway has been shown to cause freezing/immobility behavior, while activation of the VMHdm/c-to-AHN pathway rather promotes avoidance and induces immobility to a lesser extent.
source: Specifically, selective activation of the VMHdm/c-to-PAG pathway has been shown to cause freezing/immobility behavior, while activation of the VMHdm/c-to-AHN pathway rather promotes avoidance and induces immobility to a lesser extent (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: It is possible that fresh saliva-activated neurons send inputs to the PAG, whereas old saliva-activated neurons send inputs to the AHN and/or other projection sites.
source: Although the number of cFos-positive cells in the dPAG did not seem to correlate with the intensity of freezing behavior in any saliva exposure group in our study (Figure 5F), it is possible that fresh saliva-activated neurons send inputs to the PAG, whereas old saliva-activated neurons send inputs to the AHN and/or other projection sites.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on prior literature and the current findings.

claim: The number of old saliva-activated cells in the VMH may correlate with different aspects of defensive responses, rather than freezing behavior.
source: Thus, the number of old saliva-activated cells in the VMH may correlate with different aspects of defensive responses, rather than freezing behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the lack of correlation with freezing for old saliva.
